title: Adaptive throttle and SLO first-response runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is an on-call friendly, bite-sized runbook for common API failure profiles we keep seeing in production: client-facing timeouts, HTTP 429s (rate limits), degraded streaming responses (partial chunks / stalls), and sudden elevated error rates (5xx). The focus here is first-response actions, short mitigations to restore SLOs, and next-step owners for follow-up.

Scope / assumptions:
- Applies to public Redwood API (edge fleet) and Dedicated routing layer.
- We assume responder has runbook access, PagerDuty, and cluster-read permissions.
- Quick mitigation is preferred over deep debug during high-severity incidents.

High-level incident classification (quick):
- Timeouts: median latency spikes above SLO (p50/p95 crossing) and many client-side socket timeouts.
- 429s: elevated rate-limit responses from gateway or model backend, often correlated with token burst or cascading retries.
- Degraded streaming: partial or zero streaming chunks for >10% of requests, client-side stalls >5s between chunks.
- Elevated error rate: 5xx spike sustained for >5m or error budget burn >50% in 1h.

First-response checklist (0-15 minutes):
1) Acknowledge pager + set Slack channel (#sre-incident) + create short incident thread with title + severity.
2) Capture quick telemetry:
   - Check API gateway dashboards: request rate, 429 rate, backend error rate, p50/p95 latency.
   - Query time-series: graphite/Prometheus panels: api.requests.* api.errors.* api.latency.*.
   - Run these quick commands (kubectl/ops CLI):
     - ops infra tail logs-ingress --filter gateway=api-gateway -n prod 15m
     - ops telemetry query "sum(rate(api_requests_total[5m])) by (route)"
   - Identify if single route/model or broad cross-route.
3) If client-visible SLO is failing, flip to mitigation mode (do shortest effective action).

Mitigation playbook by symptom:
A) Timeouts (end-to-end request timeouts):
- Signs: socket timeout events, p95 latency >> baseline, CPU/GPU not saturated but queuing high.
- Quick actions (ordered):
  1) Check upstream model pool health (ops infra pool-status) and queue depth for KV caches. If a specific model variant is slow, route traffic to a compatible replica/model variant via routing override.\ 2) Increase short-term concurrency limit for affected pool (if autoscaling stuck) and trigger immediate scale-up: ops infra scale pool <pool-id> --scale 2x --ttl 10m.
  3) Enable degrade-mode: reduce max tokens or force shorter generation defaults for public gateway (temporary policy) to drop average latency.
  4) If backend timeouts persist, enable fallback policy to a lower-capacity but stable model (configured in routing policies as fallback: model-small-v2).
- Communications: mention affected routes and ETA for mitigation in Slack.
- Follow-up owners: infra -> investigate autoscaler logs, serving-runtime -> examine kernel stalls.

B) 429s (rate limit rejections):
- Signs: rapid increase in 429 count, often accompanied by client retry storms.
- Quick actions: 
  1) Confirm source of 429: edge rate limiter vs upstream model quota. Dashboards: limiter.hit_rate, limiter.queue_length.
  2) Short-circuit global throttles if safe: temporarily increase global rate limit for tier=prod by +20% using admin-console or ops CLI: ops throttle set global --multiplier 1.2 --reason "incident emergency".
  3) If 429s from a single tenant, isolate that tenant by applying stricter burst limits and add a short-term blocking rule to protect platform.
  4) If client retry patterns detected, engage SE/CS to contact customer (if external) and ask to back off. Post-incident: roll out more sensible retry guidance and jittering in docs.
- Safety: avoid unlimited increases; monitor CPU/GPU and error rates after change.

C) Degraded streaming (stalls / truncated chunks):
- Signs: client logs show long pauses between stream chunks, partial outputs with no final token.
- Quick actions:
  1) Identify if degradation is at proxy (ingress) or model runtime: compare ingress-to-kernel latency correlation panels.
  2) If ingress-side, restart a small subset of proxy pods behind LB (rolling restart of 10%): kubectl rollout restart deploy/api-proxy -n prod --max-unavailable=1.
  3) If runtime-side stalls, disable streaming for affected routes and serve full-response (non-stream) fallback temporarily to preserve correctness. Update headers: X-Serve-Mode: non-stream (config change).
  4) If KV-cache eviction is causing stalls, increase cache size or pin hot keys for a short period (serving-runtime team action).
- Note: streaming fallbacks will increase tail latency; communicate to product/ops.

D) Elevated error rates (5xx spikes):
- Signs: sustained error % above SLO, stack traces show consistent failure class (OOM, assertion, grpc errors).
- Quick actions:
  1) Narrow scope: are errors concentrated to single cluster/region/model? Use telemetry by region/model.
  2) If OOM/eviction-related: reduce batch sizes and force smaller batch windows in serving layer. Example command: ops serving update-config --batch-window-ms 10 --max-batch 8 --selector pool=pool-x.
  3) If widespread and unknown cause: open universal fallback route to 'safe' model (models-fallback) and enable automitigate flag.
  4) If API gateway shows malformed requests causing crashes, enable strict request validation and drop suspect payloads while logging.
- After mitigation, set incident owner for deep postmortem.

Escalation & communications:
- PagerDuty severity mapping (work in progress): Sev3 = partial degradation, Sev2 = customer-visible SLO broken for >10% customers, Sev1 = platform-wide outage.
- Notify product and CS for customer-impacting mitigations. Keep Slack channel updated every 15 minutes until stable.
- Use incident template in Confluence for timeline and decisions.

Short commands cheat-sheet (sane defaults):
- Check rate/latency: ops metrics get api.request_rate --window 5m; ops metrics get api.p95_latency --window 5m
- Restart small set of proxies: kubectl rollout restart deploy/api-proxy -n prod --max-unavailable=1
- Scale pool quickly: ops infra scale pool <pool-id> --scale 2x --ttl 10m
- Enable fallback route: ops routing set-fallback --route /v1/generate --target model:small-stable --ttl 20m
- Update throttle multiplier: ops throttle set global --multiplier 1.2 --reason "incident emergency"

Post-incident (owner actions):
- Owner: create incident ticket with timeline, root-cause hypothesis, and list of mitigations tried.
- Metrics to capture for postmortem: request_rate, error_rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, 429_rate, streaming_chunk_interval distribution, model-kernel queue depth, autoscaler decisions.
- Suggested fixes: refine retry guidance, add circuit-breaker at client-proxy boundary, implement adaptive per-tenant backpressure, improve observability for streaming chunk intervals.

Operational notes / open questions:
- We need a safe default throttle multiplier and a playbook for when increasing global throttle causes backend errors (what to do if error rates rise after increasing throughput?). TODO: formalize thresholds.
- Investigate adding a streaming heartbeat metric (chunk-heartbeat) to detect stalls earlier.
- Confirm whether ops CLI has permission guard for "ops throttle set global" in PROD — add audit log step.

Appendix: quick links and references:
- SLO dashboard: https://telemetry.redwood.example/dashboards/api-slos
- Incident template: https://confluence.redwood.example/display/ENG/Incident+Template
- Retry guidance doc: https://confluence.redwood.example/display/DEV/Retries+and+Backoff

Notes to self (rough):
- Keep this doc short and actionable; move deeper analysis to postmortem.
- Share with serving-runtime and infra leads for validation.
- Once validated, convert key plays into automated runbook actions (playbook runner).

End of draft runbook.
